newsitem.title: USA: Ohio corn and soybean crops remain mostly good.
newsitem.headline: Ohio corn and soybean crops remain mostly good.

text.p: The following is the weekly crop summary released by the Ohio Agricultural Statistics Service based on conditions as of Sunday, August 3.
Temperatures ranged from around 50 to 98 degrees. Temperatures averaged 71.3 degrees for the week ending Sunday, August 3. This is 2.9 degrees below the previous week and 1.0 degrees below normal.
Precipitation averaged 0.41 inches, 0.41 inches below normal, for the week. Growing degree days for the past week was 5 points below normal.

Reporters rated 5.9 days suitable for fieldwork during the seven day period that ended on Friday, August 1. Since the first week of April, Ohio's farmers have had 5 more days suitable for fieldwork than the five year average. Compared to last year, growers have had 19 more days suitable for fieldwork since the first week of April. As of Friday, August 1, reporters rated the topsoil moisture as 11 percent very short, 22 percent short, 64 percent adequate, and 3 percent surplus.

Ohio's average corn development stage for the majority of the corn is 15 to 16 (tassel) leaves fully emerged. Due to favorable weather conditions, corn silked rose 40 points from last week, but is behind the 1992-1996 average by about 3 days. The West central and the Central districts are still most advanced. In some parts of the State, corn ears are starting to show signs of dough stage.

Soybean blooming increased 11 points from last week. This is 5 days ahead of the five year average. The Northwestern and the West central districts are still most advanced. Soybean setting pods is a couple of days ahead of the 1992-1996 average and over 2 weeks ahead of last year.

Oats ripe increased 27 points from the previous week. Oats harvested increased 35 points from last week. Oats harvesting is 3 points ahead of the five year average and is a couple of days ahead of last year at this time.
Winter wheat harvesting rose 13 points and is 1 point ahead of the five year average. This year's harvesting progress is behind 4 of the previous 5 years.

Second cutting of alfalfa hay is 20 points ahead of last week. This is a little over 5 days ahead of the five year average and almost a week ahead of last year. Second cutting of other hay is 6 points ahead of the 1992-1996 average. Third cutting of alfalfa hay is 2 points
behind the five year average, but is 6 points, or 7 days, ahead of last year. Third cutting of other hay increased 2 points from last week.

Tobacco topped moved up 1 point from last week. Summer apple harvesting also moved up 1 point from last week. Summer apple harvesting is 2 weeks behind the 1992-1995 average. Potato harvesting reached 2 percent complete and is 7 days behind the five year average and 4 days behind last year.

Activities throughout the State included mowing hay, ditches, winter wheat stubble, and pastures; bailing hay and straw; hauling and spreading manure on wheat stubble; scouting fields; cultivating soybean fields; spraying herbicides and pesticides; tiling fields; fence and building maintenance; repairing and preparing machinery for harvest; and attending and preparing for county fairs and the State fair. Growers are harvesting tomatoes, sweet corn, and peppers. In the northern part of the State, growers are harvesting peaches.

Some reported weed pressures for the State were common and giant ragweed, Canadian thistles, Eastern black nightshade, hemp dogbane, johnsongrass, and other grass and broadleaf weeds. Some reported insects were European corn borer in corn, Mexican bean beetle and grasshoppers in soybeans, Potato leafhopper in alfalfa, and corn flea beetle in sweet corn. Reported diseases were leaf blotch on peppers, blight on tomatoes, blue mold on tobacco, and powdery mildew on pumpkins. One reporter mentioned some home gardeners were calling in about wilt in melons and pumpkin vines.

Crop conditions changed slightly from the previous week, except oats, which increased 13 points in the good category. Compared to last year, most all crops are still in better condition. A few reporters mentioned the corn is under some stress due to the heat and dry weather. The bottom corn leaves are starting to brown. Hay and pasture conditions changed slightly from the previous week. There were reports of slow hay and pasture growth and stress due to weather conditions. Some reporters mentioned the livestock were staying in the barns to avoid the warm weather.
